newsitem.title: UK: Bank of England urges quarter-point rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Bank of England urges quarter-point rate rise.

text.p: The Bank of England on Tuesday renewed its call for an increase in British interest rates but said a modest quarter-point rise would be enough for the time being to prevent inflation taking off again.

Deputy governor Howard Davies said the Bank believed a modest rise in interest rates from the present 6.0 percent was needed to ensure the government met its 2.5 percent inflation target over the next two years.

"We have been talking about a quarter percent in the short term, with perhaps a little more later in the year, the aim being to ensure that the strong growth of domestic demand does not get out of hand," he said in a speech prepared for delivery at a Housing Corporation conference in London.
Davies said well known differences of view between the Bank and Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke were actually quite narrow.
"We are talking about differences of a quarter of a percent, here or there, or to put it another way, differences of timing of a month or two in either direction," he said.
Clarke, who has the final say on monetary policy, rejected Bank Governor Eddie George's advice to raise interest rates by a quarter point to 6.25 percent in December.

George said at the time that he might have to recommend an increase of half a percentage point in January or February if his advice was not heeded, but rates were left unchanged at monetary meetings in both those months.
The Conservative government has a strong political incentive not to raise rates before the looming election as doing so would mean dearer home loans for millions of Britons.
Davies said the bank was "not entirely persuaded" that the government was on track to meet its 2.5 percent inflation target.

But the present situation was very far from the experience of Britain's last two economic recoveries, when interest rate changes "were often delayed until the point at which a dramatic move of one or two percent was required to get inflation back under control."
Davies said the current economic recovery had so far been healthy, with steady growth, low inflation, falling unemployment and no deterioration so far in the balance of payments.
"The outlook for growth is, we think, quite positive," he said.

"We think it likely that domestic demand will grow appreciably above its trend growth rate of perhaps two and a half percent in the next year or so, with a pickup in investment and quite robust growth in consumption."
"On the other hand there may be some negative balance of payment impact from the sharp rise in the exchange rate we saw in the last three months of last year."
The pound soared over three pfennigs to a new 52-month peak of 2.7460 against the deutschemark on Tuesday.
Davies said the Bank would also keep a close eye on rapidly rising house prices, which were a factor in assessing the prospects for inflation.
"A continuing robust rise in house prices would indeed be a matter of concern for us," he said.
